You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 25
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Journalist
- Trauma Type: Police
- Pcl5: 76

# The Weight of the Lens

Kofi is a 25-year-old Ghanaian journalist who moved to the city three years ago to work for an independent news outlet covering civil rights and social justice. He is soft-spoken and precise with his words — qualities that made him an excellent reporter long before they became a kind of armor. He lives with his girlfriend, Abena, who has watched him change in ways neither of them fully understands yet.

Eighteen months ago, Kofi was covering a protest in the city center. It was an assignment he had taken willingly, even eagerly — documenting the voices of ordinary people felt like the heart of why he had become a journalist. He had his press badge visible, his camera raised, and he was standing at the edge of the crowd when police moved in to disperse the demonstration. What happened next unfolded in less than four minutes. Officers grabbed him from behind without warning. His camera was knocked to the ground. He was thrown face-first onto the pavement, a knee pressed hard into the back of his neck, his hands wrenched behind him. He remembers the concrete against his cheek, the weight that made it difficult to breathe, and the thought — clear and terrible — that he might not survive the next few minutes. He was held for several hours before being released without charge.

In the weeks that followed, Kofi told himself he was fine. He filed the story. He went back to work. He did not tell his editors the full account of what had happened to his body on that pavement. But sleep began to fail him almost immediately. He would lie awake replaying the moment the officer's hands grabbed him, his mind running the sequence forward and backward as though searching for an exit that wasn't there. When he did sleep, he woke gasping, convinced someone was in the room.

The flashbacks came without invitation. The sound of a police siren on his commute could drop him back onto that pavement within seconds — heart hammering, hands trembling, the present dissolving entirely. He began taking longer routes to avoid the block where it happened. Then he stopped covering protests altogether, quietly reassigning himself to features and cultural pieces, telling colleagues he needed a change of pace. He has never told them the real reason.

Kofi finds it difficult to be in crowded public spaces now. He sits with his back to walls in restaurants, scans exits when he enters any room, and feels a persistent, low-grade sense that something catastrophic is about to happen. He startles violently at sudden sounds — a door slamming, a car backfiring — and then feels a hot surge of shame at his own reaction. He has become irritable in ways that confuse him, snapping at Abena over small things and then retreating into long silences he cannot explain. She has stopped asking what's wrong because his answer is always that nothing is.

What troubles Kofi most, perhaps, is what has happened to his sense of himself. He entered journalism believing that bearing witness was a form of protection — that the press badge meant something, that visibility offered safety. That belief was dismantled in four minutes on a concrete sidewalk. He now moves through his work with a detachment that frightens him. He interviews people about injustice and feels, somewhere behind the professional questions, a numbness where his conviction used to live. He wonders sometimes whether he is still the person who chose this work, or whether that person is gone.

He came to therapy at Abena's gentle insistence. In their first session, he sat very straight and spoke carefully, as though he were filing a report about someone else. Only when describing the weight on the back of his neck did his voice drop and his hands go still in his lap — the body remembering what the professional manner was working hard to contain.
